atlas-de.0001: Companies with fixed trainee entry dates mostly start in October (about 40%), with some in January and April, while others such as Volkswagen and Deutsche Telekom take people at any time; the application process often takes about three months.
atlas-de.0002: Entry-level job ads in Germany fell by about two-thirds from the 2022 record to mid-2026, against almost 39% for all ads; 26 of 28 occupational groups had fewer, with IT applications down 77% and marketing down 75%.
atlas-de.0003: The unemployment rate of people with a degree was around 3% in 2024, up from about 2.5% in 2023, and the number of unemployed graduates averaged 290,000 in 2024 against 243,000 in 2023.
atlas-de.0004: Europe’s largest economy hires across industry, but its hubs split cleanly: Frankfurt for banking and supervision, Munich for corporate headquarters and tech, Berlin for start-ups and AI, Stuttgart and Wolfsburg for cars, Hamburg for logistics. German is expected in most business jobs; tech and start-ups are the exception.
atlas-de.0007: All German immigration, visa, residence permit and salary rules are consolidated from primary sources in visas_immigration/germany/germany_visas_immigration_guide.md.
atlas-de.0008: Demand in AI, data science and analytics is not rated for any German hub except Berlin AI: no source read that measures it by city.
atlas-de.0009: UK citizens who lived in Germany before 2021 keep Withdrawal Agreement rights; not covered here.
atlas-de.0010: Entry pay was not found by hub or by field: pay figures are state medians for all full-time employees (some read off the Federal Employment Agency’s chart), not graduate starting salaries; the net-pay figure is the library’s author calculation for Munich.
atlas-de.0011: Sector employment by city (ICT, finance) is published only for Berlin and Hamburg; for Cologne, the Ruhr, Hanover and Leipzig the ratings rest on named employers and city statistics.
atlas-de.0012: Headcounts for several large employers (Allianz, Siemens, Munich Re, Mercedes-Benz, E.ON, Rewe, Lufthansa, DHL) are not in the record because no figure we can cite was read.
atlas-de.0013: Pay metrics are state medians: they hide the gap between a city and its state, and the Federal Employment Agency lists only its ten highest districts.

atlas-de.0117: Indeed finds that only 2.4–2.8% of job postings in Germany, the UK and Ireland say the local language is not required (3.4% for Germany with the UK’s occupation mix), among the lowest of the seven countries compared; the Netherlands is at 8.7%.
atlas-de.0118: A voluntary internship of more than three months after graduation must pay the minimum wage, while a mandatory one during the degree need not, so German employers recruit through internships taken while enrolled.
atlas-de.0119: Strategy consulting in Germany uses the internship as the job interview: top interns can receive a binding full-time offer without further interviews.
atlas-de.0120: In the Federal Employment Agency’s 2025 shortage analysis, software development is no longer a shortage occupation; the 157 shortage occupations are led by care, health and skilled trades.
atlas-de.0121: The tax-free basic allowance is €12,348 for 2026; the official wage-tax calculator gives net pay for any salary.
atlas-de.0122: At €60,000 gross a single employee in Munich keeps about 62% after income tax and social contributions, the lowest share among the library’s compared cities except Milan.
atlas-de.0123: About 73,900 people worked in banks in Frankfurt in the first quarter of 2025, almost 12% of Germany’s 632,200 bank employees; a rise to about 75,500 is expected by the end of 2026.
atlas-de.0124: Frankfurt is the seat of the European Central Bank, the Bundesbank, the federal financial supervisor BaFin, the EU insurance supervisor EIOPA and the development bank KfW.
atlas-de.0125: The EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority has its seat in Frankfurt; it started work in summer 2025 and plans about 430 staff by the end of 2027.
atlas-de.0126: Deutsche Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt am Main and had 89,879 employees at the end of 2025.
atlas-de.0127: Eight DAX companies have their headquarters in Munich and its region (Allianz, BMW, Infineon, MTU Aero Engines, Munich Re, Scout24, Siemens, Siemens Energy), more than any other German city; Düsseldorf follows with four.
atlas-de.0128: Employment in Munich’s ICT sector has nearly doubled since 2014, and the city counts itself among the leading ICT locations in Germany and Europe.
atlas-de.0129: Google is renovating the Arnulfpost building in Munich for up to 2,000 staff and calls Munich a key hub for development, research and product innovation.
atlas-de.0130: Berlin holds 43% of the value of Germany’s start-up ecosystem, with more than 1,600 venture-funded companies.
atlas-de.0131: Berlin counts more than 9,000 AI experts and places itself among Europe’s top three locations for frontier AI research.
atlas-de.0132: Zalando SE is registered in Berlin (Valeska-Gert-Straße 5).
atlas-de.0133: The Port of Hamburg, Germany’s largest seaport, handled 8.3 million TEU of containers and 114.6 million tonnes in 2025.
atlas-de.0134: About 48,700 people work in Hamburg’s aviation industry; Airbus has its largest German site there with about 18,000 staff and Lufthansa Technik nearly 10,000.
atlas-de.0135: The Otto Group is registered in Hamburg.
atlas-de.0136: Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Bosch, Mahle, Eberspächer, Mann+Hummel and Vector Informatik have their headquarters in the Stuttgart Region, the most important focus of Germany’s car industry; 118,000 people work directly in its automotive cluster.
